en: The Sūtra on Skillful Reverence, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling at the place where the Tathāgata had formerly practiced.
In the Palace of Jewel Adornments, at that time,

the World-Honored One was surrounded on all sides by a great assembly of bhikṣus, various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of the fourfold congregation, as they gathered together for the preaching of the Dharma.

At that time, the Elder Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his ten fingers in palms-together gesture toward the Buddha. With body and mind full of reverence, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata has often said that those who possess much learning have great merit;
if one further teaches others to establish a place for such learning, World-Honored One,
how much merit would that son of good family obtain?
Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying: “Ānanda!
Since you have questioned me regarding this matter, I shall provide you with an analogy to explain it.
Why is this? Because the wise attain understanding of a meaning through analogies.

Ānanda! It is as if, in this great trichiliocosm, all the trees, hundreds of flowers, and medicinal herbs—whether small or large, even those as thin as a single finger—that grow from the earth, all possess branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds in their entirety.
Ānanda! Among all those trees, even the smallest, which would be the size of a single finger’s breadth, the number of flowers and fruits produced by them is like the sands of one Ganges River.

As for the flowers, leaves, fruits, seeds, and branches produced by a tree the size of a single finger’s breadth, the number of flowers, fruits, and seeds produced by a tree the size of two fingers’ breadth is like the sands of two Ganges Rivers.

In this manner, proceeding in succession, there further arises from the ground [a tree] as wide as three fingers, which likewise possesses a certain number of branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, equal in quantity to the sands of three Ganges Rivers.
"Ānanda! What do you think? Is there anyone who could count the number of those trees?
Ānanda replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
At that time, the Buddha again addressed Ānanda, saying:
"As for all the flowers, fruits, and seeds upon even a single finger of those [trees], someone might still be able to count how many there are."

Furthermore, those sons or daughters of good family who teach others even a single four-line verse, revealing it to them without seeking any karmic reward, and who, having given rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, even teach others so that they may attain the fruit of arhatship.
Again, he thought:

"By what skillful means can I cause many sentient beings, through the power of these causes and conditions of the gift of Dharma, to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, even up to attaining the fruit of arhat, and even to resolve upon the mind of bodhi?"
Out of compassion, one teaches others even a single four-line verse, explaining it for them and analyzing it to reveal its meaning.

If one were to compare this merit with the amount of merit from the previous analogy, the former would not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, a ten-billionth part, a *kalā* part, a figurative part, or even an *upaniṣad* part of the latter; the merit of those [former acts] is incalculable.

Ānanda! Those men and women have acquired much wholesome root, even to the point of causing others to abide in great learning, and further being able to proclaim even a single four-line verse to others.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, the Venerable Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
It is truly marvelous that the World-Honored One is able to speak in such a manner.”
"How marvelous, O Bhagavān!
It is truly fitting that the Tathāgata should speak thus.
World-Honored One!"
Regarding those sons and daughters of good family who receive this Dharma, what kind of reverent mind should they cultivate toward this Dharma and the Dharma teacher?
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying: “Ānanda!
Do not question me regarding such matters.”
"Why is this? Because at present, sentient beings lack a heart that reveres the Dharma.
Ānanda then addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!

I thirst for the Dharma and have conceived a profound heart of reverence for this teaching. I study the Dharma according to the Dharma; yet since I have served as the World-Honored One’s attendant, I have never before heard such a teaching as this.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, I shall maintain such a heart of reverence as the World-Honored One has commanded, and I shall not contravene the holy teaching!
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the future final age, there may be sons of good family or daughters of good family who, regarding all dharmas, possess a semblance of thirsting aspiration, reverence, and respect, yet consist merely of words. For the sake of clothing and food, or for the sake of gain and offerings, they shave their heads and leave the household life from among the poor and lowly, and speak thus:
‘I am able to act for the sake of the Dharma,’ even though they merely seek after the Buddha-dharmas.”
"World-Honored One!
Yet those sentient beings lack a mind that practices the Dharma; they manifest the appearance of lowliness, and these people, in turn, give rise to a lowly mind.
World-Honored One!"
"I ask this question for my own sake: how should we dwell?
How should we practice?
Having spoken these words, the Buddha then addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying:

“Ānanda! If there are sons or daughters of good family who delight in the Dharma and wish to read and recite it, those beings should go to where their preceptors (upādhyāya) and teachers (ācārya) reside.”

Having arrived, one should inquire about the words of the Buddhas; then, according to what the mind finds pleasing and what it is capable of, one should state the basis for dependence (*niśraya*). Whether they have ten years of seniority or twelve years of seniority, for the sake of honoring the Dharma, one should request dependence.
Why is this? Although the Tathāgata spoke in the past, saying:
"Bhikṣus who have completed five summer retreats need not rely upon a teacher."
Furthermore, that student, through the respectful mind previously cultivated, is able to act for the sake of the Dharma;
for this reason, one should rely upon them.
Why is this? Because that person desires to study the Buddha-Dharma.
“Ānanda! Those preceptors and ācāryas should provide for him such dependence as this:
‘Is it thus? Do I permit you? Have you obtained benefit? Am I instructing you?’”
"You should be diligent and compliant; do not be heedless; you should practice with refinement; thus should you grant it.

If a bhikṣu has attained the complete dharma, he is then capable of granting dependence to others. If one can thus discern the phrases of the dharma and grant dependence to others, he is called a preceptor (niśrayācārya).
"If there is a bhikṣu who, even though he has been ordained for a hundred years, cannot freely understand such verses of the Dharma, he too must rely upon others for his dependence. Why is this?"
If one does not even understand this oneself, how much less could one wish to act as a preceptor (*niśrayācārya*) for others?

Even if an elder monk of a hundred years of seniority (*varṣa*) cannot understand the secret matters of the Śākya-son śramaṇas, that person should still grant reliance for the sake of the Dharma; likewise, even if there are elder monks of a hundred years of seniority who do not understand the Vinaya, they too should grant reliance.
"If there are bhikṣus who receive the Dharma from others, those bhikṣus should give rise to a mind of reverence and respect toward their teacher.

When desiring to receive the Dharma, they must not laugh lightly in the presence of the teacher; they must not show their teeth, nor cross their feet, nor look at the feet, nor move the feet, nor dangle their legs; the ankles should be kept level and even, without being unevenly raised or lowered."
One must not ascend a high seat in the presence of that teacher;
one must not speak abruptly unless the teacher has first posed a question;
and in all matters for which one is commissioned, one must not disobey his commands.
Do not look directly at the teacher’s face; remain three cubits away from the teacher. When commanded to sit, sit immediately and do not disobey the instruction.
Once you have sat down properly, you should arouse a mind of loving-kindness toward that teacher.
If a disciple wishes to receive the Dharma, they should kneel before the teacher and first recite what they have already learned.
If, after reciting, they have doubts, they should first consult and inform the teacher;
only when permission is granted should they request a resolution.

"At that time, once the student has received the Dharma, they should place their right knee on the ground, cup their hands over the teacher's feet, and with single-minded devotion prostrate at the place where the teacher resides.
If the ground is level and even, one should immediately pay respect;
if the ground is uneven or narrow, one should instead stand back until the teacher passes by to a level spot, at which point one may request the teaching."
When he reaches level ground, having prostrated at the teacher’s feet, he steps back and proceeds for a distance of ten cubits.
Having prostrated from afar to the teacher, he may then return as he pleases.
Furthermore, the disciple should think:
"The teacher is behind me, observing my right and wrong; I must not be negligent.
If I come immediately and go before the teacher to request a resolution of my doubts, that would be excellent."
"If you should fail to come, you must know the proper time.
One should attend to the teacher's movements three times each day; if one does not attend to his movements during these three periods, the teacher shall discipline him according to the Dharma.

"Furthermore, when a disciple goes to visit their teacher, if they do not see the teacher upon arriving at the teacher's location, they should take a clod of earth, or a piece of wood, or a blade of grass, and leave it as a sign of their presence."
If one should see the teacher within his room, at that time the student should arouse a sincere mind, circumambulate the room three times, prostrate toward the teacher, and only then return.
"If one does not see the teacher, all communal affairs must cease and may not be performed, except for the acts of defecation and urination.
Furthermore, a disciple must not speak harshly to the teacher, nor should they respond in kind when the teacher rebukes them."
When the teacher sits or lies upon the bed, one should first spread and wipe it to ensure it is free of dust, filth, insects, ants, and the like.
From the time the teacher sits or lies down until the teacher rises, one should engage in the practice of recitation.

At that time, the student, having reached the morning hours, would go to the teacher's location; once he had well understood the proper timing, he would frequently approach the teacher to inquire about what was required, asking, "What task shall I perform?"
One should address the teacher, saying:
"Shall we enter the village?
If the teacher wishes to enter the village, one must first wash one's hands and then respectfully offer the teacher's *kāṣāya* robe.
When the hand-washing is finished, one should take up one’s own robe and wipe one’s hands with it.

Upon arriving before the teacher, one should remain composed in body and mind, hold the robe with both hands, kneel for a long time to present it, and respectfully offer it according to the Dharma while remaining settled in the proper place.

Thereafter, one should offer water to wash the hands and face; first offer the undergarment to be worn against the body, and only then should one offer the other garments used for daily wear. Toward the teacher, one should maintain such a mind of reverence.

"Furthermore, a disciple must not weep or spit in the presence of the teacher. When walking within the monastery, out of respect for the teacher, one must not cover the shoulders with the *kāṣāya* nor wear it over the head."
The place where the teacher walks for meditation should always be swept and wiped clean.

If the weather is hot, one should fan the teacher three times each day with a fan, offer water three times to bathe him, and likewise present cold drinks at the three periods of the day. One should know the proper timing and go out to beg for food on behalf of the teacher.
Regarding the tasks undertaken by the teacher, one should assist in performing them with all one's physical strength. One should take the teacher’s alms-bowl, wash it, and clean it until it is pure.
If the teacher asks for assistance in washing, one should first wash the teacher’s vessel and only then attend to one’s own bowl.
If one is offered what should be washed and it is not given, one should not ask for it again.
Why? Because there is a specific reason for this.
Ānanda! There may be bhikṣus who think:
"In the past, when the Tathāgata had no one to wash his bowl, those who train in the Buddha's way ought to perform such service themselves."
"Nevertheless, although the Tathāgata has granted him permission, when it is hot, he should provide cold water;
when it is cold, he should prepare warm water;
indeed, whatever may be required should be fully prepared."
When one's parents or teacher are present, do not chew tooth-sticks;
in the presence of others, do not speak of the teacher's faults;
if you see the teacher from afar, rise immediately to greet him.

“Ānanda! Whoever has a teacher—whosoever they may be from whom one learns even a single four-line verse, whether by hearing it, reading it, questioning about it, or consulting them regarding that four-line verse—it is that person who is one’s teacher.”

At that time, those students should always give rise to a mind of reverence and respect toward their teacher; if they do not do so, they are called disrespectful and are not said to abide in right practice.
If one speaks of the teacher’s faults to others, that person shall not take me as their teacher.
Why is this? Ānanda!
Because they lack a heart of reverence, they do not love the Buddha;
because they are not even practitioners, how much less could they love the Dharma?
Since they have no respect for those who honor others, they will not love the Dharma; such great evildoers also do not love the Sangha and are not counted among the ranks of the Sangha.
Why is this? Because those foolish people do not practice the right conduct, Ānanda!
"Everything spoken by the Buddha is for the sake of practitioners.
At that time, having heard the Buddha's words, the Elder Ānanda wept with tears streaming down his face; he wiped them away with his hand and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In future ages, there will be few sentient beings who abide in this practice, World-Honored One!
We shall practice such a way; we shall now abide in such a way."
"Bhagavān!

If there is a bhikṣu who does not give rise to a heart of reverence toward his teacher or preceptor, but instead speaks of their faults and shortcomings, what kind of retribution will he receive in a future life?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If in a future age there are bhikṣus who, toward their teachers or preceptors, do not give rise to reverence but instead speak of the faults and shortcomings of those masters, such persons are neither stream-enterers nor ordinary worldlings; those deluded people should be disciplined in this manner."
Why is this? Ānanda!
If a teacher actually has faults, one may not even speak of them; how much less so when there are none!
“Ānanda! If there is a bhikṣu who is disrespectful toward his teacher, I declare that there is a separate minor hell called ‘The Beating’ (Tui-po), into which he shall fall.”

Having fallen into that place, they possess four heads on a single body; their entire bodies are likewise like masses of fire, emitting great and fierce flames that blaze incessantly, burning again and again after having already burned.
In that hell there are further insects called *hūṅ-śu* (hook-jaws); those venomous insects constantly devour the root of the tongue.

When that foolish person eventually casts off that body and is reborn among animals, he takes the form of a wild beast—either the body of a jackal (*śṛgāla*) or the body of a wolf (*vṛka*). Those people who see him cry out loudly, some shouting "Wolf! and others shouting "Jackal!"

Ānanda! Those foolish people all did so because in the past they reviled and insulted their teachers and preceptors; therefore, all who see them find them unpleasant. Due to the transgression of their tongues in the past, they constantly consume excrement and urine.
After casting off that body, although they are born among humans, they are always born in border regions.

Having been born in border regions, they abandon all matters of merit and virtue, becoming fully possessed of evil dharmas and separated from all wholesome dharmas. Although they obtain a human body, their skin does not resemble that of a human; they cannot possess the complete physical form of a person, do not resemble their parents, and are loathed by their parents.
Having obtained a human body, they will constantly be subjected to contempt, slander, and humiliation; separated from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they will forever lack wisdom.
After dying there, they will swiftly fall back into the midst of the hells.
Why is this? Ānanda!

If there are persons who give rise to disrespect toward their teachers of instruction, their teachers of mastery, their teachers of the practice of the Dharma, or their teachers of true practice, they will receive this heavy retribution.
Ānanda! Those foolish people will further encounter immeasurable and boundless states of suffering and affliction. Ānanda!

If one hears from another even a single four-line verse, or copies it, or writes it down on bamboo or silk—carrying all the names [of the teachers] upon the shoulders of those various *upādhyāyas* and *ācāryas* for many kalpas, sometimes bearing them on one's back or holding them upon the crown of one's head, constantly carrying them while walking, and furthermore using all kinds of musical instruments to make offerings to these teachers.

Ānanda! Even by performing such deeds as these, one still cannot fully repay the teacher’s kindness, nor can it be called deep reverence for the teacher; how much less so for reverence toward the Dharma!
To act with such reverence is what is called honoring the teacher. Ānanda!
Even if one possessed immeasurable and boundless articles for offering, only then would one be truly capable of making offerings to the teacher!

“Ānanda! In future ages, there will be many bhikṣus who, having obtained this sutra, will give rise to disrespectful thoughts toward their teachers and preceptors; they will lack correct practice and will constantly speak of the faults of their teachers and preceptors.”
Ānanda! I say that those foolish people will undergo extreme suffering and will certainly fall into the evil realms in a future life. Ānanda!
I declare to you, I tell you: while the Tathāgata was in the world, he has already fully explained to you that "this is the right path" and "this is not the right path";
furthermore, whatever conduct those bhikṣus practice in future ages, they will be reborn in such places and obtain such karmic fruits.
Therefore, Ānanda!
I instruct you all to constantly practice reverence. Ānanda!

If there are good men or good women who can give rise to a mind of reverence and respect, they shall attain such supreme and exalted dharmas as these: namely, loving and honoring all Buddhas and World-Honored Ones, revering and cherishing the sutras and the Dharma, and deeply loving and honoring the Sangha; they shall enter this sequence.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*The Sutra on Skillful Reverence*.
